mainEntity.name: Do flexible dentures need adhesive to stay in place?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most cases, well-fitted flexible dentures do not require adhesive. The design relies on the conforming fit of the thermoplastic material against the gum tissue, atmospheric pressure, and the grip of the flexible clasps around adjacent teeth. However, if the fit of a denture deteriorates over time — which can happen as gum and bone tissue change — a temporary denture adhesive may be used as a short-term measure while a professional adjustment or reline is arranged. Persistent reliance on adhesive is usually a sign that the denture fit needs professional attention.

mainEntity.name: How long do flexible dentures last?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lifespan of flexible dentures varies depending on care, the patient's individual oral changes, and usage patterns, but many flexible dentures provide good function for around five to eight years. Over time, changes in the jaw bone and gum tissue following tooth loss can affect the fit and retention of the denture. Regular dental reviews allow your dentist to monitor fit and recommend relining or replacement as appropriate. There are no guarantees of a specific lifespan, as each patient's circumstances are different.

mainEntity.name: Can flexible dentures be repaired if they crack or break?

acceptedAnswer.text: Repairing flexible dentures can be more complex than repairing conventional acrylic dentures. The thermoplastic nylon material does not bond in the same way as acrylic, meaning standard denture repair techniques may not be directly applicable. Some specialist dental laboratories are experienced in working with thermoplastic materials, and repairs may be possible depending on the nature of the damage. Your dental team can advise you on the most appropriate course of action. In some cases, replacement may be the recommended option.

mainEntity.name: Will flexible dentures affect my speech?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is common for any new denture — including flexible dentures — to cause minor changes to speech initially. The tongue, lips, and facial muscles need time to adapt to the new appliance, and some patients notice a slight lisp or change in pronunciation in the early days of wearing their denture. For the majority of patients, speech normalises naturally within a few weeks as the mouth adjusts. Reading aloud at home can be a helpful exercise during the adjustment period. If speech difficulties persist beyond the expected adjustment period, it is worth mentioning this to your dental team at your review appointment.

mainEntity.name: Are flexible dentures suitable for replacing all missing teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flexible dentures are most commonly used as partial dentures — to replace one or several missing teeth in an otherwise intact dental arch. They can be used for both front and back tooth replacement. Full arch flexible dentures are less commonly provided, and in some clinical situations, a different prosthetic type may offer better functional results. Whether flexible dentures are appropriate for your individual situation depends on the number and distribution of missing teeth, the condition of any remaining natural teeth, and your gum and bone health — all of which can only be assessed during a clinical examination.

mainEntity.name: Is there an age limit for flexible dentures?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no specific age restriction for flexible dentures. They can be a suitable option for adult patients of various ages, provided the clinical conditions are appropriate. For younger adults, it is worth discussing long-term planning with your dental team, as tooth loss and jaw changes can continue over time. Older patients may benefit from a careful assessment of gum health and bite before a denture type is selected. A dentist can advise on the most suitable tooth replacement approach based on your individual clinical presentation, age, and lifestyle needs.
